item.title: Fixing product search and AI shopping by fixing what the catalogue means
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an online retailer replaced inconsistent categories with a SKOS taxonomy, a small OWL core and SHACL validation, making search, filters and AI shopping reliable.
item.content:encoded:
Supplier feeds arrived with their own categories, attribute names and units. Search filters broke, facets contradicted each other and an AI shopping assistant gave confident answers from messy data. The fix was a governed product ontology that every catalogue load is mapped to and validated against.

The situation

An online retailer sold products from many suppliers. Each supplier feed brought its own category tree, attribute names and conventions: one sent "colour", another "color_name", a third put colour in the title. Sizes, materials and units varied by feed. The internal category tree had grown by accretion, with near-duplicate branches and categories that meant different things to different teams.

The symptoms were familiar. Filters returned partial results because half the products lacked the attribute being filtered. Search relied on hand-maintained synonym lists. A new AI shopping assistant made the problem more visible: asked to compare products, it reasoned confidently over data that was inconsistent underneath.

What had to be true

  • One model of meaning for categories and attributes, shared by search, filters, feeds and the assistant.
  • Mapping, not rewriting: supplier data is mapped to the model, with the original preserved.
  • Validation on every load, so bad data is caught before customers see it.
  • Business ownership: merchandisers change the taxonomy through review, without engineering in the loop for every edit.
  • Standards, not a bespoke format, so the model outlives any one tool.

Architecture

The taxonomy was modelled in SKOS, which is designed for concept schemes with broader and narrower relations and preferred and alternative labels1. A deliberately small OWL core covered the classes and properties that needed formal definitions2. The reasoning behind that split is in SKOS vs OWL for enterprise taxonomies.

The data flow, end to end

SHACL describes the conditions data must meet and produces a validation report, which made it a natural release gate for each load3. Patterns for writing shapes are in SHACL validation for knowledge graphs.

The hard part: attributes, not categories

Agreeing a category tree was comparatively quick. Agreeing attributes was not, because attributes are where search filters and assistant answers actually come from. The work that made a difference:

  • Attributes defined per category, with required, recommended and optional tiers, so a shape knows what "complete" means for a sofa versus a shoe.
  • Controlled value lists with preferred and alternative labels, so "navy", "dark blue" and supplier codes resolve to one value while search still matches all of them.
  • Canonical units with conversion at load, never in the search layer.
  • Duplicate and variant handling, the same product from two suppliers, which is an entity resolution problem in its own right; see entity resolution for knowledge graphs.

An AI assistant is only as consistent as the attributes it reads. Many apparent "hallucinations" about products turn out to be faithful readings of contradictory data.

How the engagement ran

Product pages also emitted schema.org Product markup generated from the same model4, so structured data for external search stayed consistent with internal search. More in structured data for AI search.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
SKOS for the taxonomyFull OWL ontologyLabels and hierarchy are what categories need; easier for the business to own
Small OWL coreNo formal model at allPrecise definitions where products are compared and filtered
SHACL as a load gateAd hoc scripts in the pipelineDeclarative, standard rules with readable reports
Keep supplier originalsOverwrite on mappingMappings can be corrected and replayed
Assistant reads structured attributesAssistant reads raw descriptionsComparisons and filters grounded in validated facts

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start from search logs and the categories that matter commercially, and make validation a gate rather than a report. Differently: put merchandising ownership and the review workflow in place before the model grows, not after. A taxonomy without a clear owner drifts back to where it started.

item.title: Giving KYC analysts cited answers from policy, without giving up control
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a bank gave KYC analysts a cited, permission-aware policy assistant: hybrid retrieval, evaluation sets signed off by compliance and auditable answers.
item.content:encoded:
Onboarding analysts were searching hundreds of policy pages and past case notes for every decision. The goal was an assistant that answers from approved sources only, shows its citations, respects who is allowed to see what, and is measured against questions compliance has signed off.

The situation

A bank's onboarding analysts spent much of each case looking things up. Policy lived across hundreds of pages of procedures, risk appetite statements and local addenda, and the most useful guidance was often in past case notes: how a similar ownership structure or jurisdiction had been handled before. Senior analysts carried that knowledge in their heads; newer analysts asked them, or searched a document portal that matched keywords and returned whole documents.

Customer due diligence obligations come from the FATF Recommendations and their national implementations, which require institutions to identify and verify customers and beneficial owners1. None of that changes because an assistant exists. The aim was narrower and more useful: help analysts find the right rule and the right precedent faster, with the evidence in front of them.

What had to be true

  • Answers come from approved sources only, and every answer cites them.
  • Entitlements are enforced at retrieval: a user only ever sees passages they could already open in the source system.
  • The analyst decides. The assistant informs a decision; it never records one.
  • Quality is measured before release, against questions compliance agrees are representative.
  • Everything is auditable: question, retrieved sources, model version and answer.

Architecture

The pattern is retrieval-augmented generation: a retriever selects relevant passages and a generator answers conditioned on them, which keeps knowledge in an index that can be updated without retraining2. The work was in making each layer governable.

The data flow, end to end

Hybrid retrieval mattered because KYC questions mix exact terms (a form name, a jurisdiction, a document type) with paraphrase. Keyword search finds the former and vectors the latter. The detail is in hybrid search for RAG and choosing embedding models.

The hard part: permissions that survive retrieval

The tempting shortcut is one index for everyone and an instruction to the model not to reveal restricted material. That is not access control. OWASP's Top 10 for LLM applications lists sensitive information disclosure and vector and embedding weaknesses as distinct risks for exactly this kind of system3. The approach was:

  • Carry the source system's permissions onto every chunk at index time, and re-sync them when they change.
  • Apply the entitlement filter inside the retrieval query, so restricted passages are never ranked, let alone sent to the model.
  • Treat case notes as more sensitive than policy by default, with access scoped by business line and region.
  • Test it: evaluation cases that ask, as a restricted user, for content they should not see, and fail the release if anything leaks.

The same thinking applies to retrieved text as untrusted input; see prompt injection defence.

If a user could not open the document, the model should never read it on their behalf. Enforce that in the query, not the prompt.

How it ran

Framing the work against the NIST AI RMF's govern, map, measure and manage functions gave risk and compliance teams a familiar structure for their review4. The release checklist followed RAG to production, and the evaluation design followed evaluation sets that predict production.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Entitlement filter in the retrieval queryPrompt-level instructionsRestricted content never reaches the model; testable
Hybrid keyword and vector searchVector-only retrievalKYC questions mix exact terms with paraphrase
Cite or declineBest-effort answersAn uncited answer is not usable as evidence
Compliance-owned evaluation setEngineering-owned benchmarksThe people accountable for the outcome define the bar
Pinned model versionsAlways-latest modelChanges are deliberate, evaluated and logged

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write the evaluation set before the first prompt, and put entitlements in the data path from day one. Differently: start the source clean-up sooner. Superseded policy versions and inconsistent case notes caused more wrong answers than the model did, and fixing content is slower than fixing code.

item.title: Scaling a payments platform past a million transactions a day without double charges
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a payments platform scaled past 1M+ transactions a day without double charges: idempotency keys, a transactional outbox and event-driven reconciliation.
item.content:encoded:
As volume grew, retries and timeouts started producing duplicate charges and a growing manual reconciliation queue. The goal was a payment path that was safe to retry at every step, published events reliably, and reconciled itself, sized for more than a million transactions a day.

The situation

A payments platform processing card and bank transfers for merchants was growing quickly. The architecture had served it well at lower volume: a payments service writing to Postgres, calling external providers, then publishing an event for the ledger and notifications. As traffic climbed towards and past 1M+ transactions a day, the edges started to fray. Mobile clients retried on timeouts. Providers occasionally responded slowly and then succeeded anyway. Events were sometimes published for writes that rolled back, or not published for writes that committed.

The symptoms were familiar: occasional duplicate charges, refunds issued by hand, and a reconciliation team matching provider settlement files to internal records in spreadsheets.

What had to be true

  • Every step safe to retry, from the client to the provider call.
  • One source of truth per payment, with state changes that cannot be lost or invented.
  • Reliable events: published exactly when the database change commits.
  • A ledger that balances, and reconciliation that runs itself for the normal cases.
  • Operable by the in-house team, with clear signals when something drifts.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The edge followed the IETF Idempotency-Key header draft, which defines how clients make non-idempotent methods such as POST fault-tolerant1, and borrowed conventions familiar from established payment APIs, such as rejecting a reused key with different parameters2. The full pattern is in idempotent payments and order pipelines.

The hard part: the ambiguous middle

Duplicates at the edge are the easy case. The hard case is a request that times out somewhere in the middle: did the provider charge or not? The design handled it explicitly:

  • The payment state machine had an "unknown" state for ambiguous provider outcomes, rather than guessing success or failure.
  • Unknown payments were resolved by querying the provider, never by blindly retrying a charge.
  • Provider calls carried their own idempotency keys, so a retry that did happen could not create a second charge on the provider's side.
  • Events were produced through a transactional outbox: the change and the outbox record commit together and a relay publishes afterwards, which removes the dual-write problem without distributed transactions3. The relay used Debezium's outbox event router to turn outbox rows into routed Kafka events4.

Because the relay can deliver a message more than once, every consumer was idempotent too, keyed by event ID. CDC details are in change data capture and event streams.

Exactly-once is not a property you buy from a broker. It is what you get when every producer is reliable and every consumer is idempotent.

How the engagement ran

Every hop carried a trace context, so a single payment could be followed from the client request through the provider call, the outbox, the ledger posting and reconciliation when something looked wrong.

Service level objectives and alerting followed SLOs and error budgets for small teams.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Idempotency keys at the API edgeDeduplicate downstreamStops duplicates before any side effect happens
Transactional outbox with CDCWrite to database then publishEvents exist if and only if the write committed
Explicit unknown stateTreat timeouts as failuresAvoids both double charges and lost payments
Postgres as the payment source of truthEvent-sourced paymentsFamiliar to the team; strong transactional guarantees
Automated reconciliation with exceptionsManual matchingScales with volume; people handle only real anomalies

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: name the ambiguous states in the data model and design for them explicitly. Differently: build reconciliation earlier. It is the system that tells you whether everything else is working, and it is the first place a new failure mode shows up.

item.title: Finding coordinated fraud rings with entity resolution and a knowledge graph
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a fintech moved beyond row-by-row fraud rules: streaming entity resolution into a graph of customers, devices and payees, with graph features for risk scoring.
item.content:encoded:
Fraud rules scored one transaction or one account at a time, while organised fraud spread across many accounts sharing devices, addresses and payees. The goal was to resolve those shared entities, connect them in a graph, and give risk models and investigators the network view the rules were missing.

The situation

A fintech offering accounts, cards and small loans had a mature rules engine and a transaction-level risk model. Both looked at one event or one account at a time. The losses that hurt most came from coordinated activity: clusters of new accounts opened from the same few devices, with addresses written slightly differently, paying out to a shared set of payees. Each account looked unremarkable alone. The pattern only appeared when someone noticed the connections by hand, usually after the money had moved.

The question was how to make those connections visible automatically, fast enough to matter, without replacing the decisioning stack that already worked.

What had to be true

  • Resolve before you connect: one entity per real person, device, address and payee.
  • Explainable links: every edge in a ring traceable to the evidence behind it.
  • Features, not a new decision engine: graph signals feed existing models and rules.
  • Fresh enough for onboarding and payouts, the two moments where stopping fraud pays.
  • Investigators in the loop, able to confirm, split or merge entities.

Architecture

Confirmed fraud outcomes from closed cases were fed back as events too, so proximity to known fraud stayed current and the risk models had better labels over time.

The graph model was kept deliberately small, a handful of entity and relationship types with clear definitions, following the approach in ontology vs knowledge graph vs semantic layer.

The data flow, end to end

Current entity state was held in compacted topics, where Kafka retains the latest value for each key, so downstream services could rebuild their view without replaying full history4. Streaming patterns are in change data capture and event streams.

The hard part: entity resolution you can defend

Matching everything to everything is quadratic, so resolution started with blocking: cheap keys that limit comparisons to plausible candidates, a well-studied family of techniques1. Matching then used a probabilistic, Fellegi-Sunter style model of the kind implemented in Splink, which scores each comparison field and can be trained without labelled pairs2. What made it defensible:

  • Every merge stored the field-level evidence and score, so an investigator could see why two records became one entity.
  • Thresholds were set separately for automatic merges and for "possible match" links that investigators saw but models treated with caution.
  • Shared infrastructure entities (a popular office address, a carrier-grade NAT IP) were flagged so they did not collapse unrelated customers into giant false rings.
  • Analyst merges and splits were written back as overrides that survived reprocessing.

Ring candidates came from connected components over the resolved graph, which groups nodes reachable from one another regardless of edge direction3. More detail in entity resolution for knowledge graphs.

In fraud work a false merge is not a modelling error, it is an accusation. Explainable matches and reversible overrides are what make a graph usable by investigators.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Probabilistic, explainable matchingExact keys onlyCatches variant spellings while keeping evidence for every merge
Graph features into existing modelsSeparate graph-based decision engineAdds signal without replacing a working decision stack
Small, defined graph modelLoad every attribute as a nodeFewer false connections and simpler queries
Batch proof before streamingBuild real-time firstValidates value on known cases before paying for latency
Durable analyst overridesRecompute from scratch each runHuman corrections are not lost on reprocessing

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with historical confirmed cases and show investigators the rings the graph would have surfaced. Differently: build the shared-infrastructure entity list on day one. It is the main source of false rings, and it is easier to design for than to clean up.

item.title: Building a reproducible real-world evidence network across external data partners
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a life sciences evidence team ran reproducible OMOP studies across external data partners: pre-specified designs, negative controls and packaged study code.
item.content:encoded:
A pharmaceutical evidence team licensed data from several partners and started every study with a new data pull and months of cleaning. The goal was a study pipeline that ran the same pre-specified design at every partner, measured its own bias, and could be re-run exactly when a regulator asked.

The situation

A life sciences evidence team answered questions about treatment patterns, comparative safety and outcomes using data licensed from several external partners: claims databases, EHR-derived datasets and a disease registry. Each study started the same way: negotiate an extract, receive files in the partner's format, spend months cleaning and harmonising, then write analysis code that only worked on that one extract. When a reviewer later asked a question, re-creating the original analysis was an archaeology project.

The partners were also reluctant to send patient-level data at all. The team needed a way to run studies where the data lived, with results the organisation would be comfortable defending to a regulator.

What had to be true

  • One common model at every partner, so study code runs unchanged.
  • Design before data: protocols, cohorts and analyses pre-specified and locked before results are seen.
  • Bias measured, not assumed, using controls with a known answer.
  • Exact reproducibility of any result, months or years later.
  • Data stays with the partner; only reviewed aggregates come back.

The FDA's framework for its real-world evidence programme frames the questions such evidence will face, including whether the data are fit for use and whether the study design can provide adequate evidence1. Those questions shaped the architecture from the start.

Architecture

Analytics used OHDSI's HADES packages, open-source R tools for characterisation, population-level effect estimation and patient-level prediction against the OMOP CDM2. Partner conversions followed the patterns in FHIR to OMOP architecture and OMOP vocabularies where partners started from scratch.

The data flow, end to end

Cohort practice is covered in OMOP cohort definitions, and study design choices in real-world evidence study designs on OMOP.

The hard part: proving the design is not fooling you

Observational studies can produce confident, wrong answers. OHDSI's approach to method validity uses negative controls, exposure and outcome pairs believed to have no causal effect, to measure residual systematic error, and empirical calibration to adjust confidence intervals and p-values for it3. Making that routine required:

  • A curated negative control list per study, reviewed by clinical scientists rather than generated and forgotten.
  • A rule that effect estimates stay blinded until diagnostics (covariate balance, equipoise, negative control distribution) pass.
  • Diagnostics reported per partner, because bias that appears in one data source and not another is itself a finding.

The most valuable output of a negative control analysis is permission to say "this design should not be trusted here". Building that into the process is what makes the other results credible.

How the engagement ran

Execution used Strategus, which runs HADES modules from a JSON analysis specification and restores a pinned R environment, separating study design from site-specific execution settings4.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
OMOP at every partnerHarmonise extracts centrallyStudy code runs unchanged; data stays with the partner
Locked, packaged studiesAnalysts iterate on live dataPrevents result-driven design changes; enables exact re-runs
Negative controls in every estimation studyRely on adjustment aloneMeasures residual bias instead of assuming it away
Blind estimates until diagnostics passReview everything togetherKeeps the decision to trust a design independent of its answer
Open-source OHDSI toolingProprietary analytics platformTransparent methods reviewers can inspect and partners already run

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the archived study package as the deliverable, not the slide with the hazard ratio. Differently: invest earlier in partner data cards. Knowing each source's coverage, lag and coding habits up front would have saved feasibility rounds on questions some partners could never answer.

item.title: Putting FHIR prior authorisation APIs in front of a payer's legacy claims systems
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a health payer put Da Vinci CRD, DTR and PAS FHIR APIs in front of legacy claims systems, with decision tracking and metrics reporting for CMS-0057-F.
item.content:encoded:
Prior authorisation ran on fax, phone and portals, and a federal rule had set dates for API-based exchange. The goal was standards-based FHIR APIs that providers could call, wrapped around claims and utilisation management systems that could not be replaced in time.

The situation

A regional health payer handled prior authorisation the way much of the industry still does: faxes, phone calls and a provider portal, feeding a utilisation management system that sat beside the core claims platform. Providers waited, reviewers re-keyed information, and nobody could easily answer how long decisions took or why requests were pended.

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) changed the timetable. It requires impacted payers to implement a prior authorisation API, with API compliance dates from January 2027, and to publicly report prior authorisation metrics1. Replacing the claims and utilisation management systems in that window was not realistic, so the question became how to put a standards-based front door on them.

What had to be true

  • Standards, not a bespoke API, so provider EHR vendors could integrate once.
  • No rip-and-replace: the existing systems remain the systems of record.
  • Every decision traceable, with a reason a provider could act on.
  • Humans for clinical judgement: automation handles completeness and clear-cut rules; reviewers handle the rest.
  • Metrics by construction, not by quarterly spreadsheet.

Architecture

The design followed the three HL7 Da Vinci guides that work together for prior authorisation: Coverage Requirements Discovery, Documentation Templates and Rules, and Prior Authorization Support.

CRD uses CDS Hooks so the payer can return coverage requirements inside the provider's ordering workflow2. DTR lets payer documentation rules run in the provider context so the required information is gathered up front3. PAS carries the request as a bundle built around a Claim resource, aligned to the X12 278 transaction, and is designed to be used together with CRD and DTR4.

The data flow, end to end

Status inquiries used the same decision record, so a provider checking on a pended request saw exactly what a reviewer saw, and the answer never depended on which internal system happened to hold the case.

A deeper walkthrough of the rule and the APIs is in CMS-0057 prior authorisation APIs.

The hard part: translating policy into rules people trust

The FHIR plumbing was well specified. Medical policy was not. Coverage criteria lived in documents written for human reviewers, and turning them into DTR questionnaires and rules required:

  • A policy backlog ranked by request volume, so the most common services were automated first.
  • Clinical owners for every rule, with versioning so a decision could be traced to the policy text in force at the time.
  • A firm boundary: rules could approve or route to review, but a denial on clinical grounds always went through a reviewer.
  • Specific, actionable reasons in every pended or denied response, rather than generic codes.

An API that returns "pended" faster is not an improvement. The value is in returning the right question to the provider at the moment they can still answer it.

How the engagement ran

For the security model of provider-facing apps, see SMART on FHIR authorisation; for the event backbone, change data capture and event streams.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Da Vinci CRD, DTR and PASProprietary REST APIEHR vendors integrate once across payers
Façade over existing systemsReplace utilisation managementMeets the timetable without core system risk
Versioned, owned rulesRules embedded in codePolicy changes are auditable and owned by clinicians
Clinical denials always reviewedFull automationKeeps clinical judgement with qualified people
Metrics from the event streamPeriodic reporting extractsPublished numbers match operational reality

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the decision record and event stream, because everything else (reporting, audit, provider status checks) hangs off it. Differently: bring provider-side EHR partners into testing earlier. Real Claim bundles from real ordering workflows surface mapping gaps that synthetic tests never do.

item.title: Getting an ambient AI scribe through security review and into the EHR
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a provider group moved an AI scribe past security review: private speech and LLM inference, SMART on FHIR scopes, clinician sign-off and a full audit trail.
item.content:encoded:
Clinicians were finishing notes in the evening, and every AI scribe pilot had stalled in security review. The goal was a private ambient documentation pipeline that drafted notes for clinician sign-off, ran on infrastructure the organisation controlled, and could prove what happened to every recording.

The situation

A multi-specialty provider group had a documentation problem everyone could describe: clinicians finishing notes after clinic, and patients getting less eye contact than they deserved. Ambient AI scribes looked like the answer, and several vendor pilots had been started. Each one stalled in the same place: security and privacy review. Reviewers could not get clear answers about where audio went, who could see transcripts, how long anything was kept, or how a wrong sentence in a note would be caught.

The ask was not "pick a better vendor". It was to design a pipeline the organisation could own end to end, so those questions had answers before the first recording.

What had to be true

  • Consent first: no recording without a recorded patient consent, and an easy way to stop.
  • Data stays inside the boundary: audio, transcripts and drafts processed on infrastructure the organisation controls.
  • A human signs every note: the model drafts, the clinician decides.
  • Least privilege into the EHR: the app sees the current patient and encounter, nothing more.
  • Provable history: who recorded, what was generated, what was changed, what was filed.

Architecture

The design split the problem into capture, private inference, review and filing, with audit running across all of them.

Speech recognition used a Whisper-class model, a family trained on large-scale weakly supervised audio and released with open weights1, which made private hosting practical. Note drafting ran on vLLM, whose PagedAttention memory management is designed for high-throughput serving on limited GPU memory2. Serving patterns are in LLM inference serving with vLLM and private LLMs on-premises.

The data flow, end to end

The app launched inside the EHR using SMART on FHIR, requesting only the patient and encounter context and the narrow scopes it needed3. The signed note was filed as a FHIR DocumentReference4. More on scope design in SMART on FHIR authorisation for AI apps.

The hard part: trust in the draft, not the transcript

Transcription quality was rarely the argument. The concern was a fluent note that said something the patient never said. Three choices addressed it:

  • Grounded drafting: every sentence in the draft carries a link to the transcript span it came from, and sentences without one are highlighted.
  • Clinician-scored evaluation: a curated set of consented encounters, scored by clinicians for omissions and unsupported statements, gated every model and prompt change. See evaluation sets that predict production.
  • Edit capture: what clinicians changed was recorded, so recurring corrections fed back into templates and the evaluation set.

An AI scribe is approved on the strength of its failure handling. Reviewers need to see how a wrong sentence is caught, not how rarely it appears in a demo.

How it ran

Audit records followed the shape of the FHIR AuditEvent resource (who, what, when, outcome), so the trail could be queried alongside other EHR audit data5.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Private inferenceHosted scribe APIAnswers data residency and access questions directly; costs GPU operations effort
Clinician signs every noteAuto-file low-risk notesKeeps accountability with the clinician and the model out of the record
Sentence-level source linksFree-text summaryMakes unsupported statements visible during review
Narrow SMART scopesBroad backend accessLeast privilege that reviewers can verify
Evaluation as release gateAd hoc spot checksModel and prompt changes cannot silently regress

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: take the design to the security board before building anything, and treat evaluation as infrastructure. Differently: involve clinicians in template design earlier. Most edits were about structure and specialty conventions, not model accuracy, and that work is cheaper before the pilot than during it. The broader architecture patterns are in ambient AI scribe architecture.

item.title: Turning a hospital network's EHR data into a governed real-world evidence platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a multi-hospital network turned EHR data into a governed OMOP research platform: FHIR ingestion, vocabulary mapping, data quality gates and federated studies.
item.content:encoded:
Several hospitals, several EHR configurations, and a research team waiting months for every dataset. The goal was one standardised, quality-checked research platform on OMOP, fed from FHIR, that could answer questions locally and join federated studies without moving patient data.

The situation

A hospital network wanted to use its clinical data for research, quality improvement and, eventually, AI. In practice every question became a bespoke extract: a request, a queue, a data engineer writing site-specific SQL against each EHR's reporting database, and weeks of reconciliation when the sites disagreed. The same diagnosis was coded differently between sites, lab units varied, and nobody could say how complete the data was.

The network had already invested in FHIR APIs for interoperability. The question was whether those APIs could become the feed for a research platform, rather than building yet another set of point-to-point extracts.

What had to be true

  • One model for analysis, so a cohort defined once runs everywhere.
  • Standard vocabularies, so "type 2 diabetes" means the same concept set at every site.
  • Measured quality, visible to researchers before they trust a result.
  • Privacy by architecture: identifiable data stays inside each site's boundary, and collaboration happens by sharing code and aggregates.
  • Something the internal team could run after hand-off, without a consultancy on retainer.

Architecture

The design used FHIR for extraction and OMOP CDM v5.4 for analysis, following the direction of the HL7 FHIR-to-OMOP implementation guide, developed by the Vulcan accelerator with the OHDSI community1.

The data flow, end to end

Bulk export was chosen over per-patient API calls because it's designed for population-level extraction, returning newline-delimited JSON files asynchronously2. The detailed pipeline patterns are in FHIR bulk data export pipelines and FHIR to OMOP architecture.

The hard part: meaning, not pipes

The pipeline engineering took less time than agreeing what the data meant. OMOP's standardised vocabularies map source codes to standard concepts in defined domains, which is what makes cross-site analysis possible5. Getting there required:

  • A mapping backlog ranked by how often each unmapped local code appeared, so effort went where the data was.
  • Clinician review for ambiguous mappings, recorded with reasons, rather than an engineer's best guess.
  • Unit normalisation rules for laboratory measurements, agreed with lab leads.
  • A policy for what to do with codes that can't be mapped: keep the source value, flag the concept as unmapped, and report the rate.

More on this in clinical terminologies and OMOP vocabularies.

Quality as a release gate

OHDSI's Data Quality Dashboard runs a large library of checks across conformance, completeness and plausibility4. The key decision was to treat a subset as blocking: if they fail, the new version doesn't publish and researchers keep using the previous one. The rest are published alongside the data, so researchers can judge fitness for their question. See OMOP data quality checks.

Researchers trust a platform that tells them what is wrong with it. Published quality results build more confidence than any feature list.

How a federated study runs

This is the OHDSI network model described in The Book of OHDSI3, and it is what let the network collaborate without centralising identifiable records. More in federated health analytics.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
FHIR Bulk Data as the feedDirect database extractsReuses interoperability investment; vendor-neutral; less coupling to EHR schemas
OMOP for analysisQuery FHIR directlyStandard vocabularies and the OHDSI tool and study ecosystem
Versioned CDM releasesUpdate in placeReproducible studies and safe rollback
Blocking quality checksReport-only qualityStops bad loads reaching researchers
One pilot site firstAll sites in parallelMapping lessons learned once, reused everywhere

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start from the research questions, not the tables, and make quality visible from day one. Differently: bring the vocabulary and clinical review effort forward. It's always the critical path, and it's the part that can't be bought.

item.title: Keeping secrets out of Terraform state: a checklist for platform teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Terraform state has long held plaintext secrets. Ephemeral values and write-only arguments now keep them out. A checklist to find exposure, migrate safely and harden state.
item.content:encoded:
Most organisations using Terraform have database passwords, API keys or private keys sitting in state files, often in plaintext. For years that was simply how Terraform worked. Since versions 1.10 and 1.11 it doesn't have to be, but the fix needs deliberate migration.

Ask a platform team where their production database password lives and the answer is usually "in the secrets manager". Ask where else it lives and the honest answer is often "in the Terraform state file, in plaintext, readable by anyone with access to the state bucket". That was the default for years: a secret read through a data source or set on a resource ended up in both plan and state16.

What changed

VersionFeatureWhat it does
1.10Ephemeral values and resourcesFetch or generate values during a run without persisting them in plan or state14
1.11Write-only argumentsPass ephemeral values to managed resources; never stored in plan or state2

Together they close the gap: a secret can be read from a secrets manager ephemerally and handed to a resource through a write-only argument, without ever landing in state23. There is one catch. Because Terraform never stores the value, it can't detect when it changes. Write-only arguments are paired with a version argument that you increment to trigger an update, and only the version is stored2. Support also depends on each provider, resource by resource35.

"Sensitive" hides a value from your screen. "Ephemeral" and "write-only" keep it out of the file. Only the second protects you if the state bucket leaks.

1. Find the exposure

  • Inventory every state file and who can read it, including CI service accounts and old backends nobody uses.
  • Search state for secret-bearing attributes: passwords, private keys, tokens, connection strings.
  • List data sources that read from secrets managers; each one is copying a secret into state today.
  • Treat any secret that has ever been in state as potentially exposed to everyone with state access.

2. Upgrade the toolchain

  • Move to Terraform 1.11 or later so both features are available2.
  • Upgrade providers and check their documentation for ephemeral resources and write-only arguments on the resources you use.
  • If you run OpenTofu, check its equivalent features and version support separately; the choice is covered in OpenTofu or Terraform.

3. Migrate resource by resource

  • Replace secret-reading data sources with ephemeral resources where the provider offers them.
  • Switch resources to write-only arguments for passwords and keys, with a version argument for rotation.
  • Rotate the secret as part of the migration. Moving to write-only stops future storage; it doesn't undo past exposure.
  • Better still, let the platform generate and manage the secret itself, such as a managed database credential stored in the cloud's secrets manager, so Terraform never handles it.
  • Update shared modules first, using the patterns in Terraform module design, so every consumer benefits.

4. Harden state anyway

  • Encrypt state at rest with customer-managed keys and restrict decrypt permissions.
  • Limit state read access to the pipelines that need it; humans rarely do.
  • Enable versioning and access logging on the state backend, and alert on unusual reads.
  • Keep plan files out of CI artefacts and logs, or apply the same controls to them.

5. Keep it from regressing

  • Add a policy check in CI that flags secret-bearing attributes set through normal arguments, and secret-reading data sources.
  • Document the rotation process using version arguments, so it's routine rather than tribal knowledge.
  • Include state access in access reviews and in your SOC 2 evidence; it is often the broadest secret access in the company.

How I can help

I review and redesign infrastructure-as-code estates for security and maintainability, including secrets handling, state architecture and module standards. As a fractional CTO I can own that roadmap. Or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: SLOs and error budgets for small teams: field notes on making reliability a decision, not a debate
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: SLOs and error budgets work for small teams too. How to choose SLOs, write an error budget policy, alert on burn rate and use the budget to settle priorities.
item.content:encoded:
In a small company, the argument between shipping features and fixing reliability usually gets settled by whoever is loudest that week. Service level objectives and error budgets turn it into a rule everyone agreed in advance. The Google SRE material is written for large organisations, but the core ideas scale down well.

A familiar scene in a growing company: a bad week of incidents, a tense meeting, a decision to "focus on stability" for a sprint, and then feature pressure creeps back until the next bad week. Nobody is wrong. Product wants to ship, engineering wants to stop firefighting, and there is no shared definition of "reliable enough" to settle the question.

Error budgets were designed for exactly this. The original Google SRE book frames reliability as a target to be chosen, not maximised, because every extra nine costs something5. Once the target is agreed, the gap between it and perfection is a budget the team is allowed to spend.

Start smaller than you think

Small teams fail at SLOs by trying to cover everything. Two or three objectives on the user journeys that matter most is enough to start:

  • Availability of the core API or page: the proportion of valid requests that succeed.
  • Latency for the same journey: the proportion of requests faster than a threshold users would notice.
  • Freshness or correctness for data products: the proportion of runs completed on time.

Measure at the edge closest to users, such as the load balancer or gateway, and set the first targets from what you achieved over the last month. The Workbook recommends writing the SLOs down with owners, approvers and review dates, and its example document gives each objective its own budget of 100% minus the target14.

Write the policy before you need it

The SLO is a number; the policy is what makes it matter. The Workbook says a policy should state the actions taken when the budget is exhausted and a clear escalation path for disagreements1. Its example policy is a useful template2:

TriggerExample action
Budget exhausted over the preceding four weeksHalt changes and releases other than P0 issues and security fixes until back within SLO
A single incident consumes over 20% of the four-week budgetPostmortem with at least one P0 action item
One class of outage consumes over 20% of the quarterly budgetA P0 item in next quarter's plan
Budget spent by causes outside the team's controlListed exceptions, such as company-wide network problems

For a small company, a softer version often works better: rather than halting all releases, the next sprint's capacity goes to reliability work until the budget recovers. What matters is that product and engineering leadership sign it together, before the next bad week.

The error budget's real value is political, not technical. It replaces an argument about feelings with a rule both sides agreed when they were calm.

Alert on burn rate, not on errors

Paging on every error spike burns out small on-call rotations fast. The Workbook's guidance is to alert on how quickly the budget is being consumed, combining multiple time windows and burn rates so that fast, severe problems page someone while slow leaks become tickets3. With two or three SLOs, that typically means a handful of alerts in total, each of which genuinely matters.

The telemetry comes from the same pipeline as everything else; the OpenTelemetry Collector patterns make it straightforward to compute SLIs centrally.

What changes once it's running

  • Prioritisation gets easier. Budget remaining means ship; budget gone means fix. The weekly debate shrinks to a glance at a dashboard.
  • Postmortems get sharper. Budget consumed per incident is a better severity measure than whoever shouted loudest, and pairs well with the practices in AI incident postmortems.
  • Delivery metrics gain context. DORA metrics say how fast you ship; error budgets say whether the speed is affordable.
  • Customer conversations improve. An SLO you actually meet is a far better basis for an SLA than an aspiration.

Mistakes to avoid

  1. Targets nobody would notice missing. If users wouldn't feel a breach, the SLO is measuring the wrong thing.
  2. 100% targets. They leave no budget, so every change becomes a violation5.
  3. A policy without a signature from product. Then it is an engineering wish, not an agreement.
  4. Never revisiting. Review targets quarterly, as the Workbook's document template expects4.

How I can help

As a fractional CTO, I set up SLOs, error budget policies and on-call practices that fit the size of the team, so reliability decisions stop depending on the week you're having. Or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Speculative decoding for private LLMs: faster tokens without changing the answers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation without changing outputs. How it works, when it helps on self-hosted models in vLLM, which method to choose, and how to measure it.
item.content:encoded:
Self-hosting a model gives you control over data and cost, and often a latency problem. Speculative decoding is one of the few optimisations that makes generation faster without changing what the model outputs. It also has a narrower sweet spot than its benchmarks suggest.

A common moment in private LLM projects: the model runs on your own GPUs, quality is acceptable, and users complain that answers stream slowly. Buying more hardware raises throughput but barely changes how quickly each token appears for one user. Quantisation and smaller models change the outputs. Speculative decoding is attractive because it does neither.

How it works

Generating text one token at a time leaves a large model's GPU mostly waiting on memory, not compute. Speculative decoding uses that slack. A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens; the large target model checks all of them in one parallel pass; accepted tokens are kept, and generation continues from the first rejection1.

The original Google Research paper showed this can sample from the target model's distribution exactly, so outputs are unchanged, and reported 2 to 3 times faster generation on T5-XXL with existing models and no retraining1. In practice, floating-point differences in batched GPU execution mean byte-identical outputs are likely rather than guaranteed.

Speculative decoding trades spare compute for latency. If your GPUs have no spare compute, there is nothing to trade.

The proposer options

MethodHow it proposesTrade-off
Draft modelA smaller model from the same familyGood acceptance; extra memory and a model to manage
EAGLE familyA light head trained on the target model's internal featuresStrong speedups; needs a head trained for your exact model
MTPMulti-token prediction layers built into some modelsNo separate model, where the base model supports it
N-gram / suffixCopies likely continuations from the prompt or earlier outputNo training; helps most when output repeats input

The current vLLM documentation summarises it this way: model-based methods such as EAGLE, MTP and draft models give the best latency reduction, while n-gram and suffix decoding give modest speedups without adding much work during peak traffic3. The EAGLE-3 paper reports speedups of up to 6.5 times in its experiments and argues its design lets the draft head benefit from more training data2. The vLLM project also maintains a Speculators library for training draft models that run in vLLM4.

When it helps, and when it doesn't

vLLM describes speculative decoding as aimed at reducing inter-token latency for memory-bound workloads at medium to low request rates3. That sentence is the whole story:

  • Interactive assistants with modest concurrency: good fit. Each user sees faster streaming.
  • Code editing, document revision, extraction: often good for n-gram methods, because the output repeats large parts of the input.
  • High-throughput batch jobs: weak fit. The GPU is already saturated, and verification work competes with real requests.
  • Peak hours on shared clusters: gains can fall as load rises, which is why the cheaper methods appeal.

Older vLLM releases also carried caveats, such as incompatibility with pipeline parallelism and inconsistent latency gains across datasets5. Check the documentation for your exact version rather than relying on a blog post's configuration.

How I'd evaluate it

  1. Replay real traffic, not a benchmark prompt set. Acceptance rate depends heavily on what your users ask and how your prompts are built.
  2. Measure the right latencies: time to first token, inter-token latency and end-to-end time, at your real concurrency, using the telemetry in LLM observability.
  3. Track acceptance rate and tune the number of speculative tokens; low acceptance means wasted verification.
  4. Check outputs on your evaluation set to confirm nothing changed that matters.
  5. Compare with alternatives. Prompt caching and routing easy requests to smaller models may deliver more for less effort.
  6. Decide per workload. Enable it for interactive endpoints and leave batch endpoints alone, using the serving patterns in vLLM inference serving.

How I can help

item.title: Real-world evidence on OMOP: comparing five study designs for treatment effects
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Cohort method, self-controlled cohort, case-control, case-crossover and self-controlled case series compared: what each answers, its main bias, and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
Asking 'does this drug cause that outcome?' of observational data is easy. Getting an answer you can defend is not. The OHDSI community implements five main designs for population-level estimation, each with a different way of approximating what would have happened otherwise, and each with its own blind spots.

Pharma medical affairs, payers, health systems and regulators all want the same thing from real-world data: evidence about what treatments actually do outside trials. The data, mostly claims and electronic health records, is plentiful. The hard part is design. Every observational study is an attempt to estimate a counterfactual, what would have happened to these patients without the exposure or with a different one, from data that only records what did happen1.

The OHDSI community implements five main designs for this as open-source R packages in its Methods Library, all running on OMOP data13. Knowing what each one assumes is the difference between evidence and a confident-looking chart.

The five designs at a glance

DesignComparesMain strengthMain vulnerability
Cohort method (new user)New users of target vs new users of comparatorEmulates a trial; rich diagnosticsUnmeasured confounding between groups
Self-controlled cohortExposed time vs time just before exposureNo between-person confoundingBaseline risk differing between periods
Case-controlExposure in people with vs without the outcomeEfficient for rare outcomesChoice of controls
Case-crossoverExposure at outcome time vs an earlier control timeCases are their own controlsTrends in exposure over time
Self-controlled case seriesOutcome rate in exposed vs all unexposed timeNo between-person confoundingTime-varying confounding; outcomes that end observation

All rows are drawn from the descriptions in The Book of OHDSI1.

Cohort method: emulating a trial

The new-user cohort design compares people who start the target treatment with people who start a comparator, and follows them for a defined time-at-risk. It is defined by five choices: target cohort, comparator cohort, outcome cohort, time-at-risk and model1.

The central problem is that patients on different treatments differ. OHDSI's preferred adjustment is a propensity score fitted with large-scale regularised regression over many generic characteristics, typically 10,000 to 100,000 of them, rather than a hand-picked list1. The design comes with diagnostics: preference score distributions to check the groups overlap, and covariate balance after adjustment, where some guidelines recommend standardised differences below 0.114.

The book is clear that this is inherently a comparative design. Comparing a treatment with no treatment is hard because a comparable unexposed group is difficult to define; an active comparator for the same indication is preferred1.

Self-controlled designs: people as their own controls

Three designs avoid between-person comparison altogether. The self-controlled cohort compares outcome rates during exposure with the time just before. The case-crossover design asks whether exposure was more common just before the outcome than at an earlier control time; because the outcome always comes later, it can be biased by exposure trends, which the case-time-control variant addresses. The self-controlled case series compares the outcome rate during exposed time with all unexposed time, before, between and after exposures1.

These designs are robust to confounding by stable characteristics such as genetics or chronic conditions, but vulnerable to things that change over time, such as age, season or disease progression1. The self-controlled case series also assumes the end of observation is independent of the outcome, which can fail for fatal outcomes such as stroke; an extension exists to correct for that15.

No design is assumption-free. Choose the one whose weaknesses matter least for your question, then test it on questions where you already know the answer.

Case-control: efficient, but fragile

Case-control studies compare exposure in people with the outcome against people without it, often matching on age and sex and sometimes nesting within a subgroup such as patients with the relevant indication1. They are efficient for rare outcomes, but results depend heavily on how controls are selected.

How I'd choose and validate

  1. Write the question precisely as cohorts and time windows, as in OMOP cohort definitions.
  2. Default to the new-user cohort design with an active comparator for comparative effectiveness, because its diagnostics make problems visible.
  3. Use self-controlled designs for acute outcomes after transient exposures, such as vaccine or short-course drug safety, where timing is sharp.
  4. Run negative controls. Outcomes believed not to be caused by the exposure reveal residual bias; the book's method validity chapter covers this and empirical calibration2.
  5. Replicate across databases through the federated network approach, after data quality checks at each site.
  6. Keep estimation and prediction separate. Causal questions and prediction models need different designs and different validation.

item.title: Fine-tuning a foundation model? When the EU AI Act makes you a general-purpose AI provider
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: EU AI Act rules for general-purpose AI models now have enforcement behind them. When fine-tuning makes you a GPAI provider, what the Code of Practice asks, and what to document.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies building on foundation models assume the EU's general-purpose AI rules are for the labs. Usually they are. But the Commission's guidelines draw a line where heavy modification turns a downstream builder into a provider, and since August 2026 the AI Office can enforce those rules.

Picture a scale-up that takes an open-weight model, continues pre-training it on a large domain corpus, fine-tunes it further and offers it to customers across Europe. Is it a deployer of someone else's model, or the provider of a new general-purpose AI model? Under the EU AI Act the answer changes the paperwork considerably, and it now carries enforcement risk.

This is an architect's reading of public guidance and law firm commentary, not legal advice.

Where things stand

The AI Act's obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since 2 August 2025. The Commission said the AI Office was preparing its compliance assessments ahead of enforcement of those rules from August 20262. A Cloud Security Alliance research note published on 3 August 2026 summarised the AI Office's powers as including requests for documentation, model evaluations, corrective measures and fines7.

Alongside the law sit two practical instruments. The GPAI Code of Practice, published on 10 July 2025, has three chapters: transparency, copyright, and safety and security. The first two give all GPAI providers a way to demonstrate compliance with Article 53; the third applies only to providers of models with systemic risk under Article 5516. The transparency chapter includes a Model Documentation Form1. The Commission also finalised a template for the public summary of training data5.

The line between deployer and provider

The Commission's guidelines on GPAI providers address downstream modification directly. As summarised by commentators34:

  • An indicative criterion is whether the training compute used for the modification exceeds one third of the compute used to train the original model.
  • If the original compute isn't known, one third of the threshold for presuming a model is general-purpose is used instead.
  • Minor changes typically don't make you a provider.
  • If you do become a provider, your obligations generally concern the modification: documentation, training data summary and copyright policy covering the additional compute and data. Modifying a model with systemic risk brings the full systemic-risk obligations.
What you doLikely position
Prompting, RAG, tool use, agents on a hosted modelNot modifying the model
Light fine-tuning or adapters on modest dataTypically a minor change
Large continued pre-training or extensive fine-tuningCheck the compute ratio carefully
Modifying a model already classed as systemic-riskGet specific legal advice early

Most teams are nowhere near the line. The ones that are usually know it, because they are spending serious money on GPUs. That spend should come with a compliance budget.

Why this matters even if you are well below it

First, customers ask. In enterprise procurement, "we use RAG, not fine-tuning" is a much easier answer with evidence behind it. Second, upstream providers' documentation flows down to you: the Model Documentation Form exists partly so downstream providers can understand the models they build on1. Third, the same records support obligations that apply to your AI systems regardless of the model rules, such as the literacy duty in Article 4 and the timeline in the Digital Omnibus roadmap.

What I'd put in place

  1. Log training compute for every model you train or tune, with the method used to estimate it. It's cheap to capture at the time and very hard to reconstruct later.
  2. Keep a model lineage record: base model and version, upstream documentation received, datasets, licences and changes. The supply chain practices in AI model supply chain security overlap heavily.
  3. Document data provenance and copyright handling for any data you train on, including how rights reservations are respected.
  4. Prefer adaptation over retraining where it meets the need. RAG and lighter tuning are usually cheaper as well as simpler to govern; see long context vs RAG.
  5. Map once, reuse often. Tie these records into a framework such as ISO 42001 so the same evidence serves EU, US and Gulf requirements.

item.title: Kafka queues are production-ready: when share groups can replace a separate message broker
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Apache Kafka 4.2 made queues (share groups) production-ready. How they differ from consumer groups, which workloads they fit, and when a separate message broker still makes sense.
item.content:encoded:
Many platforms run Kafka for event streams and a second system for work queues, because Kafka's consumer groups tie each partition to one consumer. Kafka 4.2 made share groups, its queue semantics, production-ready. For some teams, that means one less system to run.

A familiar architecture: Kafka carries business events between services and into the lakehouse, while RabbitMQ, SQS or a database-backed job table handles background work such as sending emails, generating documents or calling a model. Two systems, two sets of operational skills, two places where messages can get stuck. The reason was structural. Kafka's consumer groups assign each partition to exactly one consumer, so you cannot scale workers beyond the partition count, and one slow message holds up everything behind it.

What changed

KIP-932, "Queues for Kafka", introduced share groups. Kafka 4.0, the first release to run only in KRaft mode without ZooKeeper, offered them as early access45. The 4.2.0 release announcement describes Kafka Queues as production-ready, adding a RENEW acknowledgement type, adaptive batching in the share coordinator, limits on fetched record counts, and lag metrics13.

Consumer groups versus share groups

The Kafka documentation describes share groups as an alternative to consumer groups: consumers share a topic's records without each partition being tied to one consumer, records are acknowledged individually, and delivery attempts are counted. It suggests them for workloads that process records one at a time rather than as an ordered stream2.

Consumer groupShare group
AssignmentEach partition to one consumerRecords shared across consumers
Scaling limitNumber of partitionsNot tied to partition count
Progress trackingOffset per partitionAcknowledgement per record
RetriesBuilt by the applicationDelivery attempts counted by Kafka
OrderingPreserved within a partitionNot the design goal
Best forEvent streams, CDC, aggregationsIndependent tasks: jobs, notifications, AI calls

If the order of records matters, use a consumer group. If each record is an independent piece of work, a share group is now a real option.

Where it fits well

  • AI and enrichment workloads. Calling a model for each document or record is slow and variable. Share groups let you add workers to match throughput without repartitioning, and a slow call doesn't block the rest.
  • Fan-out jobs from existing events. If the events already land in Kafka, for example from change data capture, processing them as tasks without copying them to another broker removes a hop.
  • Bursty background work, where worker count needs to swing widely during the day, combined with autoscaling like that in Kubernetes scale-to-zero.

Where a separate broker still wins

  • No Kafka today. Adopting Kafka just for a work queue is rarely worth it. A managed queue is simpler.
  • Complex routing. Topic exchanges, header-based routing and per-message priorities remain stronger in dedicated brokers.
  • Strict ordering with parallelism. If you need per-key order and parallel processing, keyed consumer groups remain the right model.
  • Small clusters. Share groups store state in an internal topic that defaults to three replicas, so clusters with fewer than three brokers must adjust internal replication settings first2.

How I'd adopt it

  1. Get to a current release. Share groups need KRaft-based Kafka 4.x; plan the ZooKeeper migration first if you haven't5. Run the latest 4.2 patch release rather than 4.2.0.
  2. Pick one queue workload that already consumes from Kafka and has idempotent processing, using the patterns in idempotent pipelines. Per-record acknowledgement still means at-least-once delivery.
  3. Decide what happens after the last attempt. Route repeatedly failing records somewhere a person will see them.
  4. Monitor share-group lag with the new metrics and alert on it, as you would queue depth1.
  5. Check your managed service. Hosted Kafka offerings adopt new features and metrics at different speeds.
  6. Retire the old queue only after a full cycle of peak load and incident handling on the new one.

item.title: Running an enterprise MCP registry: a playbook for governed tool discovery
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The official MCP Registry is designed to feed subregistries. A playbook for running a private enterprise MCP registry: curation, namespaces, approvals and client rollout.
item.content:encoded:
Once a few teams adopt MCP, the question shifts from 'how do I build a server?' to 'which servers are we allowed to use?'. The MCP Registry was designed with that in mind: a public upstream that organisations can mirror, filter and extend with their own private servers.

A typical enterprise MCP adoption follows a pattern. A few engineers connect assistants to useful servers. A platform team builds internal servers for the CRM, the data warehouse and the ticketing system. Within months there are dozens of servers, nobody knows which are approved, and security finds a community server with broad file system access on a developer laptop. The fix is not to ban MCP. It is to give people a catalogue of servers they're allowed to use.

How the MCP Registry is designed

The official MCP Registry launched in preview in September 2025 as an open catalogue of publicly available servers14. Three design choices matter for enterprises:

  • Metadata, not code. Entries describe servers and point to packages in existing registries such as npm, PyPI and Docker Hub12.
  • Verified namespaces. Server names use a reverse-DNS format, such as io.github.username/server or com.example/server, tied to a verified GitHub account or domain2. That gives you a basis for trusting who published what.
  • Built to be extended. The registry and its API specification are open source, so others can build compatible subregistries that pull from it, filter it and add their own servers13.

The registry remains in preview, and its documentation warns that breaking changes or data resets may occur before general availability2. Build against it, but pin and mirror what you depend on.

The playbook

1. Decide what "approved" means

Write down the criteria before choosing tools: publisher verified, source available, package signed or pinned, permissions documented, data classification of what it touches, and an internal owner. The controls in securing MCP servers make a good starting checklist.

2. Stand up a private subregistry

Run a registry that implements the same API, so clients that understand the official registry can use yours35. Servers on internal hostnames or private package feeds belong here, not in the public registry2.

3. Mirror, don't proxy

Pull public entries into a staging area, review them, then promote approved versions. Pin to specific package versions so an upstream update can't change what your users run without review. This is the same discipline as AI supply chain security.

4. Enrich entries with your context

Add what the public registry can't know: owner, data classification, allowed user groups, required auth extension, and a link to the review record. Tool annotations and UI capabilities, covered in MCP Apps and tool annotations, should be part of the review.

5. Point clients at it

Configure managed IDEs and assistants to discover servers from your registry, and where clients support it, block unapproved sources. A catalogue nobody is pointed at is just documentation.

6. Tie it to identity

Approval should map to who can use a server. Pair the registry with the enterprise authorisation patterns in MCP extensions, so access is granted through your identity provider rather than per-server credentials.

7. Measure and prune

Track which servers are used, by whom and how often, using the telemetry approach in LLM observability. Retire servers without owners or usage, and re-review on major version changes.

A registry turns MCP from a collection of personal integrations into a platform. The governance lives in the promotion step, not the protocol.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the public registry as an allow-list. Listing proves a verified namespace, not safety.
  • Floating versions. "Latest" from upstream means unreviewed code on every laptop.
  • No owner per server. Internal servers without owners become the next unpatched dependency.
  • Registry without enforcement. If clients can still add any server, the registry is advisory only.

item.title: The UAE's new Federal Authority for AI and Data: what it means for technology teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The UAE has merged its AI office, digital government and data office into one federal authority. What has been announced, what is still unknown, and how I'd prepare.
item.content:encoded:
In June 2026 the UAE created a single federal body for AI, data governance and digital government. This week Dubai set new targets for its AI campus. For companies building or selling AI in the Emirates, the institutional map is consolidating, and that changes who sets the standards you'll be measured against.

For years, AI and data policy in the UAE was spread across several bodies: an AI office within the federal government, the digital government function inside the telecoms regulator, a data office, and emirate-level and free zone authorities alongside them. Teams working here learned to ask "which regulator?" before "which rule?". That is starting to change.

This is an architect's reading of public announcements and law firm commentary, not legal advice.

What was announced

In June 2026 the UAE approved the establishment of the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, reporting to the Cabinet, as a unified national body for data governance, artificial intelligence and digital government12. Commentary reports that it brings together three existing functions13:

Previous bodyWhat it covered
Artificial Intelligence OfficeNational AI strategy and programmes
TDRA Information and Digital Government SectorFederal digital government services and standards
Emirates Data OfficeNational data governance

The mandate described in commentary covers the national AI strategy, government data governance, and standards and compliance across federal entities13. By October, reporting on the UAE's AI programme was already framing the authority as the body bringing national data, AI and digital government systems together6.

This week: Dubai's AI campus targets

On 26 October, during the Dubai AI Festival, Dubai approved new targets for its AI campus: more than 1,000 AI companies and over 5,000 specialised jobs by 203045. Together with federal consolidation, the direction is clear: one national voice on AI and data standards, and emirate-level competition to host the companies building on them.

Consolidation usually means fewer, clearer standards, applied more consistently. Teams that have been relying on ambiguity should plan for less of it.

What we don't know yet

  • Private sector reach. The described mandate centres on federal entities. How far its standards will extend to private companies, directly or through procurement, is not yet clear.
  • Interaction with free zones. DIFC and ADGM have their own data protection regimes, including DIFC Regulation 10 on AI systems. How federal AI standards will sit alongside them remains to be seen.
  • Data protection supervision. The federal PDPL continues to apply. Which body leads on its AI-related aspects will become clearer through guidance.
  • Health data. Sector rules, such as those in the UAE health data law, remain in place.

The regional pattern

Saudi Arabia went down this path earlier, with the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority as a single body for data and AI7, alongside its own data protection law covered in Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI. A combined data and AI authority tends to treat data governance and AI governance as one discipline. Architecturally, that's right: most AI risk is data risk.

How I'd prepare

  1. Map your current obligations by entity and location: federal PDPL, free zone regimes, sector rules, and where your models and data actually run, as discussed in UAE AI infrastructure.
  2. Build governance on a recognised framework, such as ISO 42001 or the NIST AI RMF, so national standards become a mapping exercise.
  3. If you sell to government, expect federal data and AI standards to appear in procurement first. Keep an AI system inventory and data lineage ready to evidence.
  4. Unify data and AI governance internally. If the regulator treats them as one discipline, a separate AI committee disconnected from data owners will struggle.
  5. Watch for guidance from the new authority and plan a quarterly review of your mapping.
